newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Swiss SGS profits rise 10.9 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swiss SGS profits rise 10.9 pct.

text.p: Swiss group Societe Generale de Surveillance Holding SA (SGS) reported that first half group net profit rose by 10.9 percent and it expected the positive trend to continue, barring any major foreign exchange deterioration.
SGS, the world leader in inspections and testing, also said its U.S. insurance services unit GAB Robins North America Inc was breaking even and expected to return to profitability in 1997.

SGS consolidated revenues rose 8.6 percent to 1.40 billion Swiss francs ($1.1 billion) during the first half of 1996, while net profit grew by 10.9 percent to 110.9 million francs. Internal growth nearly doubled to 9.5 percent compared with the previous period.

"In the current environment and barring any major foreign exchange rate deterioration, this positive trend should be sustained for the remaining part of 1996," SGS chairwoman Elisabeth Salina-Amorini said in a letter to shareholders.
Serge Pahud, chief financial officer, told a news conference: "We are confident about a good second half-year.
"The second half of the year is generally better for us, so logically results should improve," he added.

A buy-back of 300,000 registered shares from Union Bank of Switzerland, approved by SGS shareholders last June and representing 3.4 percent of SGS share-capital, should result in a higher dividend per share this year, the chairwoman said.
Salina-Amorini, speaking to a news conference, said: "The results reflect good progress in our main business segment, inspections, where profits rose by 12 percent.
"They also reflect a return to equilibrium in our services to the insurance industry, notably GAB," she added.

SGS's insurance industry services posted an operating loss of 12 million francs during the first six months of 1995, but ended the six months to June 1996 with a loss of just 200,000 swiss francs, according to Salina-Amorini.
The sector represents 18.7 per cent of total group revenues worldwide.
"GAB management is confident that this company will return to profitability in 1997," she added. "But it is a long job and there is no quick fix."
New government contracts, which globally represent more than 20 per cent of SGS revenues, have been signed with Paraguay, the Central African Republic and Guinea.
Pahud said three service sectors -- in environment, non-destructive testing and logistics (customs transit) posted a combined loss of 10 million swiss francs for the period. ($1=1.2427 Swiss Franc)
